slides.label: Title
slides.notes: Open by grounding the lecture in PDF page 197, where the chapter announces the shift from reflection as an example to reflection as the seed of every orthogonal operator. The promise for students is that products are no longer bookkeeping: they become reusable geometric programs.

slides.label: Reflection Sandwich
slides.notes: Emphasize that the reflecting vector has two readings. It is still a drawable direction, but when placed on both sides of an object it becomes an operator. The visual target is component behavior: the part aligned with the mirror survives while the complementary part changes sign.

slides.label: Two Reflections
slides.notes: Walk through the order slowly: the rightmost reflection acts first, and the product of the two mirror vectors stores the whole operation. The half-angle is the important geometric surprise. A small angle between mirrors produces twice that angle on any vector in the plane.

slides.label: Rotor Sandwich
slides.notes: Present the sandwich as an interface, not just a formula. Once the rotor is unit length, the reverse supplies the inverse, and the same expression can rotate a vector, an oriented area blade, or a product of objects. That is the coding payoff of the algebra.

slides.label: Bivector Planes
slides.notes: Students often import axis-angle intuition too early. Recenter the picture on the bivector plane, because the plane is what multiplies like the imaginary unit and what appears in the exponential. In three dimensions the familiar axis is available by duality, but it is not the stored generator.

slides.label: Rotor Sign
slides.notes: Use the plot as a diagnostic rather than as a curiosity. A vector endpoint returns after one full turn, but the rotor has moved to negative identity. That sign matters whenever the path is continuous, especially in animation, tracking, interpolation, or controller state.

slides.label: Composition Order
slides.notes: The key habit is to read rotor products like composed functions. The rotor nearest the object acts first after the sandwich expands. Stress that both orders can pass basic orthogonality checks, so a frame picture or a basis-image ledger is needed to catch order bugs.

slides.label: Versor Parity
slides.notes: Define versor broadly enough that rotors become one case rather than the whole story. The parity of the vector-factor count controls orientation behavior. That lets students classify an operator before expanding it, and it prepares them for odd reflections and higher-dimensional even versors.

slides.label: Subspace Operators
slides.notes: Make the object-operator dual reading explicit. A blade may represent a plane that can be inspected, but the same algebraic element can also define a reflection. The important invariant is structural: transformed wedges agree with wedging transformed factors, so constructions move coherently.

slides.label: Complex And Quaternion Links
slides.notes: Use this as a translation slide. Complex numbers and quaternions are not abandoned; they are explained as low-dimensional rotor coordinates. The gain is conceptual and practical: the multiplication rules come from geometric products, and the same idea can move beyond the dimensions those classical systems cover.

slides.label: Rotor Log Interpolation
slides.notes: Connect logarithms to interpolation rather than treating them as formal decoration. The log extracts the bivector angle that generates the relative rotor. Scaling that bivector gives meaningful intermediate operators, and the same interpolated rotor can act on a vector path and a blade path together.

slides.label: Rotation Diagnostics
slides.notes: Frame diagnostics as small invariant questions. Norm preservation catches scaling errors, determinant sign catches parity mistakes, basis images catch order mistakes, and log coordinates catch the intended plane and angle. The goal is to debug the operator as a geometric object, not as a mysterious array.

slides.label: Debugging Lab
slides.notes: Use this as a short active pause. Students should identify the scalar as the cosine of half the angle, the bivector coefficient as the signed sine term, and the plane as e12. The diagnostic is not complete until they predict and test one basis vector image.

slides.label: Recap
slides.notes: Close by tying the visual sequence back to the chapter opening. Reflections are not an isolated trick; two reflections create rotors, and products of vectors become versors. The lasting engineering message is that transformations can preserve geometric structure while staying inspectable through algebraic factors.
